market_definition.boundary_notes: Two boundaries matter and the difference between them is large. Customer support software overall is estimated at $11-14B in 2026; the e-commerce-specific slice is roughly $1.5-2B [S2]. A third boundary is emerging and cuts across both: AI agents are no longer a product line but a feature shipped as standard by the dominant vendors, with Intercom's Fin bundled into mid-tier plans [S1]. So 'AI support agent' is not a category boundary at all — it is a capability inside an existing one.
how_analysts_segment_it: By breadth: all customer support software versus the e-commerce-specific slice [S2]
By vendor scale: dominant horizontal vendors versus small players specific to e-commerce [S1][S2]
By delivery: standalone purchase versus bundled into the support suite or the commerce platform at no additional cost [S1]

sizing.consensus_view: Customer support software is $11-14B in 2026 growing 17-21%, of which the e-commerce-specific slice is roughly $1.5-2B [S2]. One source addressed sizing, so this is a single estimate rather than a consensus.
sizing.why_estimates_diverge: No two estimates were available to diverge. The gap that matters here is not between analysts but between two different objects: the whole category and the e-commerce slice within it, which differ by roughly 6-8x [S2]. A figure near $12B is credible for the former and badly wrong for the latter.

tailwinds: Support is a recurring operational cost for merchants, so automation has a measurable target
Adoption is well past experimental: the dominant vendors ship AI agents as standard rather than as an add-on [S1]
headwinds: Per-resolution pricing fell through 2025 and 2026 as platform vendors bundled the capability [S3]
Standalone vendors report compressed expansion revenue [S3]
Shopify ships native support tooling free to merchants on its platform, covering a large share of the small-merchant segment [S1]
demand_signals.buyer_budget_reality: For a large share of small merchants there may be no incremental budget at all, because the commerce platform includes support tooling at no additional cost [S1]. Where a budget exists, the realised price per resolution has been falling [S3].

saturation.consolidation_activity: None seen. No source here reports an acquisition in this category.
saturation.why: Five named players, two of them dominant horizontals shipping the capability as standard and one platform giving it away free to the target segment [S1][S2]. Pricing is compressing, which is the clearest saturation signal available and the one that is directly evidenced rather than inferred [S3]. The read is 'crowded but differentiable' rather than 'effectively closed' because the e-commerce slice is a real $1.5-2B segment with its own small specialists [S2], which implies merchants do buy something beyond the horizontal tools. New-entrant flow is unknown.

absorption_risk.notes: The verdict is 'feature' at high confidence, and unusually the evidence is not a forecast: the absorption has already occurred in three places. The dominant vendors ship the capability as standard, one bundles it into mid-tier plans, and the platform gives support tooling to merchants free [S1]. The price evidence corroborates it — per-resolution pricing fell as platform vendors bundled, and standalone vendors report compressed expansion revenue [S3], which is what absorption looks like in the numbers rather than in a roadmap. No precedents are cited because none of the available sources documents a comparable case; drawing on antivirus or file sync would be my own analogy rather than research.

open_source_landscape.evidence_for_the_gap: No source in this material names an open-source support-agent project, reports adoption for one, or discusses open source in this category. `applicable` is false on that basis, and this should be read as unresearched rather than assessed. The capability_gap and gap_trend values are schema placeholders and carry no finding.
open_source_landscape.notes: The commoditization pressure in this category is documented, but it is running through platform bundling rather than through open source [S1][S3]. Filling this section with invented projects would point the reader at the wrong risk.

adjacent_markets.market: Customer support software overall (the horizontal category)
adjacent_markets.why_it_matters: The horizontal vendors have moved into the e-commerce use case by shipping agents as standard [S1], so the boundary between the slice and the whole is thinning from above.
Shopify supplies native support tooling to its merchants free [S1]. The platform is upstream of the merchant relationship and can convert support into an included feature at will.

economics.typical_pricing: Per-resolution pricing is used in this category and has been falling through 2025 and 2026 as platform vendors bundled the capability [S3]. No absolute price levels are given in the available material.

factors: No regulatory factor appears in the available research.
The structural constraint is platform dependency: a large share of the target segment reaches support tooling through the commerce platform they already run [S1].

research_gaps: Nothing establishes how capable the bundled agents are for e-commerce specifically. That is the decisive gap: 'bundled' and 'adequate' are different claims, and the size of the remaining opportunity depends entirely on which applies.
No source characterises Gorgias's or Tidio's products, so the deck's claim that they are rule-based [C2] cannot be checked either way.
No pricing levels, gross margins or CAC payback figures were available, so the economics section is unfilled rather than estimated.
No funding, valuation or acquisition data, so consolidation activity and investor appetite are unknown.
New-entrant flow is unknown, leaving one of the five saturation signals unmeasured.
Nothing addresses open source in this category.
Nothing speaks to this company's own traction [C4, C5] or to support volume for small merchants [C6].
